Two figures here are deliberately not what they look like: `verifications.daily.used` is `null` when today's count could not be read (never 0, which would read as a measured idle day), and `verifications.daily.percent` is ALWAYS `null`: there is no enforced daily quota to be a percentage of, and `used` counts emails while `limit` counts credits, which are not the same unit.

200.description: Usage this billing period.

plan.description: `{id: "sub_account", name: "Sub-account"}` for a white-label sub-account, which has no plan of its own.

remaining.description: The spendable WALLET, not `limit - used`: the balance is the only thing enforcement checks, and purchased packs sit outside the plan grant.

resets_at.description: When the allowance refills: the end of the billing period. `null` with no billing period, and `null` when the plan is set to end at the close of this period, since nothing refills it then. A time already past means a renewal is due; the refill lands when its payment is recorded.

used.description: `null` when today's count could not be read. Not zero: a fabricated idle day is worse than an honest unknown.

limit.description: The plan's published daily credit number. NOT enforced anywhere; do not size work from it.

remaining.description: The wallet again, for the same reason as the monthly figure.

percent.description: Always null. There is no enforced daily quota, and `used` (emails) and `limit` (credits) are different units.

rate_limit.description: Requests per minute the limiter holds this credential to. When no live window describes the request, the plan's limit, or for a white-label sub-account its own limit (never its parent's plan's).

rate_limit_enforced.description: False means the number beside it is the configured limit rather than something being applied.

billing_period.description: The period `credits.used` and `verifications.monthly.used` cover. For a short time after a renewal, until its payment is recorded, the counter has not been reset: it holds the previous period's spend and anything spent since, and this covers the same stretch, from when the counter was last reset up to now.

get.description: Credits, API calls, verifications and bulk-job concurrency for the current billing period.

200.description: The summary.

data.description: The canonical usage shape. @see shared/contracts/usage.ts, which the dashboard and the Lambda both compile against.

balance.description: Spendable now. Fractional: a cached verification costs 0.5.

used_this_month.description: What it measures depends on `allowance_basis`: the current billing period for `billing_period`, and a cumulative figure for every other basis (a paid plan with no billing period on file, Free, a sub-account).

allowance_basis.description: Only `billing_period` renews. `no_billing_period` (a paid plan with no billing period on file), `one_time_grant` (Free) and `provider_allocation` (a white-label sub-account) are not reset on a schedule, so the figure beside it is cumulative.

api_calls.description: Verification REQUESTS, not addresses. One 5,000-address batch is 1 request and 5,000 verifications.

daily_limit.description: Misnamed: carries the CREDIT allowance, not a call ceiling. Nothing meters API calls. Read `daily_credits`.

monthly_limit.description: Misnamed in the same way. Read `monthly_credits`.

total.description: Always `null`: a lifetime verification count is not tracked. The only all-time figure is credit spend, and publishing that as a verification count produced fractional 'verifications'.

max_concurrent.description: Not enforced. A per-plan number (1, 2, 5, 10 or 20) that nothing checks: no route counts running bulk jobs or refuses one over it, so do not throttle against it or present it as a limit. Kept for existing clients; `active` beside it is the measured count.

coverage.description: How much of the billing-period window the job-derived counts (`api_calls`, `verifications`, `bulk_jobs`) actually cover. Job rows expire at the plan's result retention, so on Free `this_month` covers the last 7 days, not the month. The shorter windows (today, this week) fit inside retention on every plan. Absent from a Lambda build that predates the field.

requested_days.description: Days from the window's start to now, rounded up (what was asked for).

covered_to.description: End of the covered window. Usually the present; a window whose billing period ended in the past ends then instead.

retention_days.description: How long the account's current plan keeps verification results.

complete.description: True when the figures cover the whole requested window.

reason.description: Why the window was shortened, or null when it was not.

billing_period.description: All three are `null` on a plan with no period, and also when a paid plan's period could not be resolved, which is unknown rather than absent. For a short time after a renewal, until its payment is recorded, `credits.used_this_month` has not been reset: it holds the previous period's spend and anything spent since, and this covers the same stretch, from when the counter was last reset up to now, with `days_remaining` 0.

partial.description: Names the sections whose counts could NOT BE READ. Their numbers are zero-filled placeholders, not measurements. Render them as unavailable, not as zero.

get.description: The account's credit ledger, newest first: the charges and refunds on the balance, each with the balance it left. After a failure that carries `retry_may_charge_again` it shows whether a debit of that amount landed around that moment, which `GET /v1/usage` (the balance alone) cannot. A row carries no request id and no address, so that settles the question only when nothing else on the account was spending at the same time; on a route that accepts one, an `Idempotency-Key` is the reliable answer. Entries before 2 September 2026 show usage and refunds only: credits added before then, from a plan or a credit pack, have no row, so `type=purchase` is empty for that period even for an account that bought credits then. From that date every paid-plan allowance and credit-pack purchase has a `purchase` row; the one-time Free signup grant is the exception, credited to the balance directly with no row.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Rows per page, 1 to 100 (default 50). A malformed, fractional, zero, negative or larger value is a 400 rather than clamped, the same `parseListLimitParam` rule as `GET /v1/analytics/credit-history` and the other list routes. Until 2026-10-02 it was clamped, and `limit=0` meant 50.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: How many rows to skip, default 0. A negative or unreadable value means 0. Above 10000 is refused with 400: the ledger is read row by row up to the offset, so the offset is what the request costs.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Return only rows of this type. `transfer` is credits moved between a white-label account and one of its sub-accounts: an allocation, a reclaim, or the balance a deleted sub-account returned. Any other non-empty value is a 400 naming the seven.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The previous page's `next_cursor`, to read the page after it. Reaches any depth, where `offset` stops at 10000, and costs one page however deep. Not combined with a non-zero `offset` (400). A cursor that does not decode, is not in the shape this route issues, or is another account's is a 400 `INVALID_CURSOR`.

200.description: One page of the ledger.

amount.description: Negative for a debit, positive for credit coming back. Fractional: a cached verification is -0.5.

description.description: What the credits were for, written by the feature that moved them. A generic label for the row's type when `detail_withheld` is true.

detail_withheld.description: Present only when a scoped credential lacks one of `verification:read`, `integrations:read`, `white_label:read` and `billing:read`, which together cover every kind of material a description can name; `description` is then generic and `reference_id` is null.

total.description: Rows matching the request, across every page.

offset.description: The `offset` the request sent; 0 for a page read from `cursor`.

has_more.description: True when another row exists after this page.

next_cursor.description: Pass it back as `cursor` to read the page after this one; null on the last page. Unlike `offset`, it reaches past the 10000th row.

get.description: Every active key on the account, with the scope vocabulary beside them so a caller that can list keys can also see what a narrower one could be limited to. Never returns a secret: `key_preview` is the stored masked form, and a key created before previews were stored shows `ev_••••`.

200.description: The keys, and the scope vocabulary.

available_scopes.description: The whole scope vocabulary, in the order a UI should present it.

sensitive.description: Marks a scope that spends money, destroys data or changes who has access. Present these differently from a read scope.

recommended_agent_scopes.description: What to give an AI agent doing list hygiene: verify, watch the job, read the result, see what it cost. Nothing that spends money outside verification credits, nothing that changes access, nothing destructive. Published here so the safe default is the discoverable one.

post.description:
The secret is returned once and never again: `data.api_key.key` is the only place it ever appears.

Accepts `name` and, optionally, `scopes`; any other field is a 400 rather than silently ignored. A new key is refused with a 400 (`Maximum of 10 API keys allowed per account`) while the account already has 10 active keys, on every plan (dashboard sign-in sessions and connected apps do not count); revoke one first. The cap is checked only here: keys suspended when a subscription ended are not counted, and resubscribing restores them, so an account can hold more than 10 that way and then cannot create another until it is under 10. `GET /v1/usage/limits` publishes the cap as `limits.api_keys`. Omitting `scopes` creates an unrestricted key. Sending `scopes` creates a key limited to exactly those scopes: an empty array is refused (a key that can do nothing is never what was meant) and so is `null` (omitted and null are not the same thing, and this route will not guess which was meant). A scope a key does not hold answers `403 INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` on use, naming what it needed.

Creating a key with a dashboard session needs a sign-in within the last 15 minutes; an older session answers `403 REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`. Creating one with an API key has no such limit, but the key used must itself be unrestricted: no scope grants minting.

name.description: A label for the key, for your own benefit. **Measured after trimming**: `handleCreate` runs `rawName.trim()` before the 1-100 length check, so a 100-character name padded with spaces is accepted and stored trimmed, while a raw `maxLength` would refuse it, and `" "` satisfies a raw `minLength: 1` and is refused anyway. The `\S` pattern stays because it is the one part that survives trimming: it requires at least one non-whitespace character.

scopes.description: Limit the new key to these scopes. Omit the field for an unrestricted key; `[]` and `null` are both 400s. A `:write` scope implies its `:read` half, so `verification:write` alone can read results. The stored list is normalized to this document's order, so the response may not list them as sent. Duplicates are accepted and collapsed: `parseRequestedScopes` inserts into a Set and returns the de-duplicated list in a fixed order, so `["verification:read", "verification:read"]` creates the same key as one entry. No `uniqueItems` here for that reason: it would refuse locally a payload the API takes. The `maxItems` limit applies to the RAW array, before de-duplication.

201.description: The new key. Save it now.

api_key.description: The only response that ever contains the secret.

key.description: THE SECRET. Returned here and nowhere else; no later call can recover it. Store it before reading the rest of this object.

key_id.description: The key's identifier, used to revoke it. Not secret.

scopes.description: The scopes the key was created with, normalized and ordered. `null` means unrestricted. Always present, so a client never has to tell 'unrestricted' from 'the field was omitted'.

examples: Save this API key now. You will not be able to see it again.

500.description:
The key could not be created and the outcome is **indeterminate**. `handleCreate` rethrows an unclassified `TransactWriteCommand` failure and the outer handler answers this, so the transaction may have committed with the response lost.

That matters more here than on most routes, because **the secret is returned once**. If the write landed, the key now exists on the account and nobody has its value: it cannot be recovered, only revoked. Do not retry blind: read `GET /v1/api-keys`, revoke anything that appeared without a secret you hold, and only then create another.

delete.description: The key stops working at once, and so do any dashboard sessions created from it. Webhooks created with the key, or from a dashboard session created from it, are switched off (`is_active: false`, `disabled_reason: "api_key_revoked"`) and stay listed until you turn them back on or delete them. They are switched off before the key is revoked: if that fails, this answers `500` and the key is not revoked, so the same request can be sent again, even with the key itself. The account's last active key cannot be revoked; create a replacement first.

200.description: Revoked.

500.description: `INTERNAL_ERROR`: the revocation may not have happened, so **the key may still be active**. Retry, and confirm with `GET /v1/api-keys` that it is gone. Once the key is revoked the answer is `200`, including when some of the rows of the dashboard sessions created from it are left to clean up later: those sessions are refused on their next use either way.

200.description: The account's endpoints.

webhooks.description: Every endpoint on the account. **Never includes `secret`**: a signing secret appears only in the successful response that creates or explicitly rotates it.

webhook_id.description: What the get, update, delete and test operations take as `{id}`.

url.description: The canonical callback URL. `null` identifies a malformed legacy endpoint that cannot deliver; repair it with PUT or delete it. One such row does not hide the account's other endpoints.

is_active.description: False means Kawaa has stopped delivering to it. Set it back with the update operation; `disabled_reason` says why when Kawaa switched it off.

updated_at.description: Falls back to `created_at` on an endpoint that has never been changed.

last_triggered_at.description: Null on an endpoint that has never fired, which is not the same as one that is failing.

failure_count.description: Consecutive delivery failures. A rising number beside a recent `last_triggered_at` is an endpoint that is being called and refusing.

disabled_reason.description: Why Kawaa switched this endpoint off: `api_key_revoked` (an API key that created it, or that pointed it at its current URL (or, when none did, changed its events or turned it on), or the key behind a dashboard session that did, was revoked) or `app_disconnected` (a connected app that created it or did one of those was disconnected, including by a password change or reset or an account lock). The endpoint is kept, with `is_active: false`, so its owner can review it and turn it back on or delete it. `null` while it is on, and for an endpoint someone switched off.

count.description: Rows returned. The quota counter behind `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` is maintained separately and is the authoritative one; this is a count of what was read.

post.description:
Kawaa POSTs to `url` when one of `events` happens, signing each delivery. Past the plan's endpoint cap this answers `403 PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. With a dashboard session, the session must have signed in within the last 15 minutes; an older one answers `403 REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED` (sign in again, then retry). An API key or a connected app is not held to this. The write is conditioned on the creating API key (or the key a dashboard session was signed in with, or a connected app's access token) still being active, so a request made just before that credential was revoked answers `401 API_KEY_REVOKED` and creates nothing. A password change, reset, account lock or white-label sub-account key reset that lands while the request is in progress answers `409 CONFLICT`; nothing is created.

**A scoped key needs more than `webhooks:write` here.** A subscription is a way to receive what its events carry, so each requested event also requires the scope that owns that data: `verification.completed` needs `verification:read`, `verification.failed` needs `verification:read`, `job.completed` needs `verification:read`, `job.failed` needs `verification:read`, `credits.low` needs `account:read`, `credits.exhausted` needs `account:read`, `blacklist.detected` needs `deliverability:read`, `dmarc.failure` needs `deliverability:read`. On an account that can have sub-accounts, `credits.low` and `credits.exhausted` additionally require `white_label:read`, because those deliveries name the sub-account and its label. Missing any of them is a `403` naming each event and the scope it needed, and no webhook is created. An unrestricted key needs none of this. `x-kawaa-event-scopes` carries the same table in machine-readable form.

url.description: Where Kawaa POSTs the callback. HTTPS only: anything else is 400 WEBHOOK_URL_INVALID. No `format: uri` or anchored scheme `pattern` is declared on this REQUEST field: `validateWebhookUrlStatic` parses with `new URL()`, which tolerates surrounding whitespace and normalizes the protocol, so `" https://x"` and `"HTTPS://x"` are both accepted while either constraint refuses them. HTTPS is required, checked on the PARSED protocol, not on the string you sent. Before storing it, Kawaa replaces the request string with that parsed URL's canonical string, so every response URL is a well-formed URI.

description.description: A note for your own reference. Send `null` to clear the stored one.

schema.description: Closed: `findUnknownField(body, WEBHOOK_CREATE_FIELDS)` allows only `url`, `description` and `events`. `is_active` is NOT one of them: an endpoint is created active, and it is the update operation that can deactivate it.

201.description: Registered. This endpoint's initial signing secret is returned once; no read operation returns it, but the rotation operation can replace a lost or exposed value.

secret.description: THE SIGNING SECRET. Every delivery to this endpoint carries `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` (and the legacy `X-Kawaa-Signature`) computed from it; without it there is no way to tell a genuine callback from anything else that can reach the URL. Save it now: no read operation returns it. If it is lost or exposed, `POST /v1/webhooks/{id}/secret` replaces it and returns the replacement once, without deleting the endpoint.

409.description: `CONFLICT`: a password change, reset, account lock or white-label sub-account key reset landed while this request was in progress, so the account no longer matches what the request was authenticated against. Nothing was created. Repeat the request if your credential still works.

500.description:
The endpoint could not be created and the outcome is **indeterminate**. The outer handler answers this when the quota read or the `TransactWriteCommand` throws, and a transport failure on that transaction can leave the write committed with no response to show for it.

This POST is **not idempotent**: it takes no `Idempotency-Key`, and a blind retry can register a SECOND endpoint that then receives duplicate callbacks for every event. Read `GET /v1/webhooks` first and retry only if the endpoint is not there.

503.description: The webhook URL's hostname could not be resolved right now (`WEBHOOK_DNS_TEMPORARY_FAILURE`). This is a TRANSIENT DNS failure, not a rejection of the URL; a permanent one is `400 WEBHOOK_URL_INVALID`. Nothing was created or changed. Retry.

get.description: Every event name, what triggers it, and an example payload. Read this rather than hard-coding a list.

200.description: The event catalogue.

events.description: Every event name a subscription may name. Read this rather than hard-coding: an event Kawaa does not know is refused at create.

available.description: **False means nothing produces this event yet, and a subscription naming it is REFUSED.** `normalizeAndValidateEvents` rejects it with 400 on create and on update, and names the available events in the message. schema.description: Send only what you are changing. `findUnknownField(body, WEBHOOK_UPDATE_FIELDS, WEBHOOK_READ_ONLY_FIELDS)` refuses the first key that is neither writable nor a known response field with 400, so a misspelling is caught, while a round trip of a fetched endpoint object is deliberately accepted. 200.description: Updated.

url.description: The canonical callback URL. This is `null` only when the update omitted `url` and the stored legacy destination was malformed; send a valid URL in another PUT to repair it.

disabled_reason.description: As on the listing: why Kawaa switched the endpoint off, or `null`. Sending `is_active: true` clears it.

updated_at.description: When this change landed. The update response carries only this timestamp: `created_at` is not returned here; read it from the listing or the single-webhook route.

webhook.description: The endpoint as it now stands, including a description cleared in this same request: the response reports the stored value for every field, so there is no need to re-read after an update. No `secret`: a signing secret appears only in the successful response that creates or explicitly rotates it.

409.description: `CONFLICT`: nothing was changed. One of: the request turns the endpoint on (`is_active: true`), and Kawaa switched it off while the request was in flight because an API key or connected app that created it, or that changed its URL or events or turned it on, was revoked or disconnected (a password change, reset or lock included): check where it sends, then send the request again to turn it on. Or the request changes `url` or `events`, or turns the endpoint on, and the account's credentials changed while it was in flight (a password change, a reset, a lock, a white-label key reset, or for a dashboard session signing out every session): send it again if your credential still works. Or another request changed the endpoint after this one read it: read it again, then send your change again if you still want it.

503.description: The webhook URL's hostname could not be resolved right now (`WEBHOOK_DNS_TEMPORARY_FAILURE`). This is a TRANSIENT DNS failure, not a rejection of the URL; a permanent one is `400 WEBHOOK_URL_INVALID`. Nothing was created or changed. Retry.

put.description:
Change an endpoint. Only the fields sent are changed. With a dashboard session, changing `url` or `events` needs a sign-in within the last 15 minutes; an older session answers `403 REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`. Sending the URL and events the endpoint already has is not a change. The same goes for `is_active: true` on an endpoint with a `disabled_reason`: turning back on an endpoint Kawaa switched off trusts its destination again. An API key or a connected app is not held to this. `is_active: true` clears `disabled_reason`, and is refused with `409 CONFLICT` if Kawaa switched the endpoint off while the request was in flight (a revoke, password change or lock that landed after it was authenticated); sending it again afterwards turns it on.

**A scoped key needs more than `webhooks:write` here.** A subscription is a way to receive what its events carry, so each requested event also requires the scope that owns that data: `verification.completed` needs `verification:read`, `verification.failed` needs `verification:read`, `job.completed` needs `verification:read`, `job.failed` needs `verification:read`, `credits.low` needs `account:read`, `credits.exhausted` needs `account:read`, `blacklist.detected` needs `deliverability:read`, `dmarc.failure` needs `deliverability:read`. On an account that can have sub-accounts, `credits.low` and `credits.exhausted` additionally require `white_label:read`, because those deliveries name the sub-account and its label. Missing any of them is a `403` naming each event and the scope it needed, and no webhook is created. An unrestricted key needs none of this. `x-kawaa-event-scopes` carries the same table in machine-readable form.

200.description: Deleted.

post.description:
Replace the endpoint's signing secret without deleting or reconfiguring the endpoint. A successful call returns the replacement exactly once; deliveries that load the endpoint afterward use it, while a delivery already in flight may still carry a signature made with the previous value. Store the returned value before leaving the response; no read operation can recover it.

**The previous secret stops working at once.** There is no overlap: every later delivery is signed with the replacement only. Until your receiver has it, it refuses those deliveries, and a 401 or any other 4xx answer is final and not retried, so events sent in that gap are not delivered on their own. If you can, have your receiver accept a signature made with either secret while the replacement rolls out, then drop the old one. Re-send what failed in the gap with `POST /v1/webhooks/{id}/logs/{logId}/retry`; a re-send is signed with the current secret.

With a dashboard session this needs a sign-in within the last 15 minutes, as changing `url` or `events` does; an older session answers `403 REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`. An API key or a connected app is not held to this. Each rotation is recorded in the audit log as `settings.webhook_secret_regenerated`, without either secret.

200.description: The secret was replaced. Subsequent deliveries are signed with this value, except that a delivery already in flight may have loaded the previous secret before rotation.

secret.description: The replacement signing secret, returned by this successful rotation only. It is now the value used for `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` and the legacy `X-Kawaa-Signature`.

500.description: The rotation outcome is **indeterminate**: the write may have committed even though its response was lost. Retrying is safe for endpoint configuration but rotates again. Retry this same operation until one call succeeds, then keep only the secret from that successful response; it supersedes every earlier value.

get.description:
The deliveries made to this endpoint, newest first: product events, test sends and retries, each with what was sent and what the endpoint answered. Entries are kept for 30 days. An entry for a `verification.*` or `job.*` event holds that job's data, so it is removed with the job's results when the plan keeps results for less time than that, and can no longer be read or retried.

**A scoped key sees only the entries whose payload it may read.** Each entry holds its payload verbatim, so an entry is returned only when the key holds the scope that owns what its event carries (`verification:read` for `verification.*` and `job.*`, `account:read` for `credits.*`, `deliverability:read` for `blacklist.detected` and `dmarc.failure`; on an account that can have white-label sub-accounts, `credits.*` also needs `white_label:read`, because those events can name a sub-account). The events left out for that reason are named in `withheld_events`, and an unrestricted key or a dashboard session sees every entry. An id that belongs to another account is a 404.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Entries per page. Default 20. A value above 100 is served as 100, and a missing, zero, negative or non-numeric value is served as 20, rather than refused; a fraction is rounded down. The response's `limit` says what was applied.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Entries to skip from the newest, default 0. A value above 1,000 is served as 1,000 and a negative or non-numeric value as 0, rather than refused. Page past that with `cursor`. Not applied when `cursor` is sent.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The `cursor` from the previous page, to read the next one. Opaque; do not construct or edit one. A cursor that does not decode, is not in the shape this endpoint issues, or belongs to another webhook is a 400 with code `INVALID_CURSOR`; start again without it.

200.description: One page of the log.

items.description: One delivery attempt run: a product event, a test send, or a retry. Each retry is a NEW entry; the entry it re-sent keeps its original outcome.

log_id.description: What the retry operation takes as `{logId}`.

event.description: The event the delivery carried, as it was stored. Entries written before the event names were settled can carry a legacy alias (`batch.completed`, `batch.failed`, `credits.depleted`) rather than its canonical name.

status_code.description: The endpoint's HTTP status. Null when no HTTP response was received (timeout, DNS or connection error, or a URL refused as unsafe); `error_message` says which.

response_time_ms.description: How long the delivery took, across its attempts. Null on an entry that did not record it.

request_body.description: The JSON body that was sent, verbatim, as a string: parse it to read the payload. The signature was computed over exactly these bytes. A test send's body carries `"test": true`.

response_body.description: The start of what the endpoint answered, truncated. Null when it answered nothing or no response was received.

error_message.description: Why a failed delivery failed, e.g. `HTTP 500`, a timeout, or `Webhook URL rejected: ...`. Null on a success.

delivery_type.description: `event` for a real delivery, `test` for a send from the test operation, `retry` for a re-send from the retry operation. Entries written before this field existed read as `event`.

count.description: How many entries are on this page.

total.description: An older name for `count`, kept for existing clients: the number of entries on THIS page, not the number of deliveries the endpoint has had, which is not counted.

limit.description: The page size that was applied.

offset.description: The offset that was applied, echoed even when `cursor` was sent and the offset was not used.

cursor.description: Present when there may be more entries. Send it back as `cursor` to read the next page; its absence is the end. A page can be shorter than `limit`, or empty, and still carry one, so page until it is absent rather than stopping at a short page.

withheld_events.description: Present only for a scoped key that may not read some events' payloads: the canonical names of the events whose entries this key is not shown. Entries for these events may exist and are not on the page. Absent when the key is refused nothing.

unclassified_withheld.description: Present when an entry was left out because its event is one this Kawaa build does not recognise, so no scope could be matched to it. Such an entry is not named in `withheld_events`. An unrestricted key is shown it.

unclassified_withheld_unknown.description: Present when the check for such unrecognised entries could not be completed, so the page may or may not have left one out. Not the same as `unclassified_withheld` being absent.

post.description:
Sends the logged entry's `request_body` again, byte for byte, to the endpoint's CURRENT URL, signed with its current secret. The re-send carries a fresh `X-Kawaa-Timestamp` header, an `X-Kawaa-Retry: true` header and an `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` whose `t` is the time of the re-send, so it passes a receiver's 300-second window however old the original is; the body, including its own `timestamp` field, is the original's. Check freshness against that `t`, never against the body's `timestamp`. It is made once, with a 10-second timeout, and recorded as a NEW log entry with `delivery_type: "retry"`; the original entry keeps its outcome. Any entry still in the log can be re-sent, a successful one included. No request body is read.

A scoped key may re-send only an entry whose payload it may read (the same rule the log listing applies); otherwise the answer is 403 and nothing is sent.

parameters.name: logId
parameters.description: The entry's `log_id`, from the delivery log.

200.description: The re-send was ATTEMPTED. **200 does not mean it worked**: branch on `data.success`.

success.description: Whether the endpoint accepted the re-send (a 2xx). False for a non-2xx, a timeout, a connection failure, and a URL refused as unsafe or missing, all of which still answer HTTP 200 here.

status_code.description: What the endpoint answered. `0` when nothing was reached.

message.description: What happened, in prose, e.g. `Retry successful`, `Retry failed with status 500`, or why the URL was refused.

404.description: Nothing was sent. `Webhook not found` for an endpoint id that is not this account's; `Log entry not found` for a `logId` that does not exist, belongs to another endpoint, or has passed its retention.

409.description: `CONFLICT`: nothing was sent. Kawaa switched the endpoint off because an API key or connected app that created it, or that changed its URL or events or turned it on, was revoked or disconnected, or the delivery check found such an end. Check where it sends and turn it back on before resending deliveries to it.

503.description: The log entry could not be read at that moment, so nothing was sent. Retrying this operation is safe. Also when the credentials the endpoint records could not be checked: nothing was sent.

post.description: Delivers a signed sample payload to the endpoint so you can confirm signature verification before real events arrive. It carries the same signature headers as a real delivery, `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` with the time of this send and the legacy `X-Kawaa-Signature`.

200.description: The delivery was ATTEMPTED. **200 does not mean it worked**: branch on `data.success`.

success.description: Whether the endpoint accepted the delivery (a 2xx). False for a non-2xx, a timeout, a connection failure, and a URL refused as unsafe, all of which still answer HTTP 200 at this route, because the REQUEST succeeded even though the DELIVERY did not.

status_code.description: What the endpoint answered. `0` when nothing was reached.

response_body.description: The first part of the endpoint's body, for diagnosing a rejection. Null when there was none.

message.description: What happened, in prose: the only place a DNS refusal or an SSRF block is explained.

event.description: The canonical event whose sample payload was delivered, and the value of the `X-Kawaa-Event` header on that delivery. Equals what you sent, with a legacy alias resolved to its canonical name, or `verification.completed` when the request named no event. Read it to confirm which integration path the test actually exercised.

Which event's sample payload to send. Omitted, the FIRST event Kawaa defines (`verification.completed`) is used, not necessarily one this webhook is subscribed to, so a test with no body can exercise an event the endpoint never receives in practice. Explicit `null` and other non-string values are refused with 400; only omission selects the default. **An unrecognised name is refused with `400 Invalid events: <name>`** (the same message create and update give), so a mistyped `dmarc.failur` fails loudly instead of delivering a `verification.completed` sample and reporting success. Legacy aliases (`batch.completed`, `credits.depleted`) resolve to their canonical names. The response's `event` field names whichever event was actually sent. Valid names come from `GET /v1/webhooks/events`.

schema.description:
Optional. `event` picks which event shape the test delivery carries; omit the body entirely and the endpoint picks one.

Deliberately NOT closed, because this route is not: it parses the body and reads `body.event`, and anything else is ignored rather than refused. That is unlike create and update, which run `findUnknownField` and answer 400 for the first key they do not recognise, so a misspelled `evnet` here still selects the default event rather than failing. The VALUE of `event` is now validated (an unknown name is a 400), so the remaining gap is a misspelled KEY. Check the response's `event` field to confirm which sample was sent. Send only `event`.

get.description:
The plan catalogue. Needs a valid API key like every other route here; `is_current` marks the plan that key's account is on.

Every `price` is quoted in `currency`, which is always USD: this endpoint does not take a currency and does not convert. `billable_currencies` is the separate question of which currencies a subscription can be created in, and `credit_package_currencies` the same question for one-off credit packs. Those two lists differ, so offering a currency from the wrong one produces a checkout the customer cannot complete.

**A white-label sub-account has no plan of its own.** The route is open to sub-accounts (it is the public price list), but such an account spends a credit pool its parent allocated and holds no subscription. It gets `current_plan: "sub_account"` (agreeing with `GET /v1/account`), `is_current: false` on every plan, and a `plan_note` saying where the subscription lives. Do not present a plan as that account's, and expect `403 SUB_ACCOUNT_MANAGED` from every subscription write.

200.description: The plans.

plans.description: Every plan, in catalogue order, free first. A sub-account is not in here: it has no plan of its own.

price.description: Per `interval`, in `currency`, in whole currency units (not cents). `0` for free.

currency.description: Always `USD` today: the catalogue is quoted in one currency. @see billable_currencies for what a subscription can be created in.

interval.description: How `price` is billed: every paid plan is billed monthly. It does not say the credits renew; read `credits_renewal` for that. Free has no price, and its credits do not renew.

credits.description: The plan's credit grant. On a paid plan it is added each billing period, when that period's invoice is paid (`credits_renewal: "monthly"`); an invoice left unpaid grants nothing. On Free it is a one-time grant that nothing renews (`credits_renewal: "one-time"`): given when the account is created, and again when a paid subscription ends (is cancelled or deleted) and the account moves back to Free. An unpaid subscription that moves the account to Free does not grant it: that subscription has not ended. Not a verification count: a cached verification costs 0.5 and a domain search 10.

credits_renewal.description: Whether `credits` renews: `monthly` on every paid plan, `one-time` on Free. The same field, with the same values, as `GET /v1/usage/plans` publishes for each plan. Absent from a Lambda build that predates it.

features.description: Marketing lines for the plan, in display order. Not a machine-readable entitlement list; read `GET /v1/usage/limits` for the enforced numbers.

is_current.description: True for the plan the calling key's account is on. False on every plan for a white-label sub-account, which is subscribed to none of them.

current_plan.description: The account's plan id, repeated here so a client does not have to scan `plans` for `is_current`. `free` when the account has no subscription. `sub_account` for a white-label sub-account, which has no plan of its own; see `plan_note`, and note that no entry in `plans` is marked `is_current` in that case.

plan_note.description: Present only when `current_plan` is not a plan the account is subscribed to: today, only for a white-label sub-account, whose subscription is held by its parent and whose credits are the pool that parent allocated. Same field, and the same purpose, as `plan_note` on `GET /v1/usage/limits`. Absent for every ordinary account.

currency.description: The currency every `price` above is quoted in.

billable_currencies.description: The currencies a SUBSCRIPTION can actually be created in, derived from the Stripe prices that exist, so it can be shorter than the supported list and can change without a deploy. A currency outside it is refused at checkout.

credit_package_currencies.description: The currencies a one-off CREDIT PACK can be bought in. Packs are priced inline at checkout rather than from a stored Stripe price, so this list is not bound by `billable_currencies` and is usually longer.

get.description:
One-off credit packs. Needs a valid API key.

Prices are quoted in `currency`, which defaults to USD and is set by the query parameter. Each pack has a price in every supported currency, so this returns one currency's prices, not all of them. A currency Kawaa cannot price is a `400`, not a silent fallback to USD: quoting dollar amounts under another currency's label is how a buyer ends up comparing the wrong numbers.

200.description: The packs, priced in the requested currency.

packages.description: Every pack, smallest first. The list is fixed; only the prices move with `currency`.

name.description: A display name built from the credit count.

credits.description: Credits added on purchase. They do not expire with a billing period.

price.description: One-off charge in `currency`, in whole currency units (not cents).

currency.description: LOWER-CASE here, unlike the plan catalogue, which reports it upper-case. Same value, two spellings: compare case-insensitively.

savings_percent.description: Discount against the smallest pack's per-credit rate, as a whole number. `null` for the smallest pack, which is the baseline.

popular.description: A display hint for the pack Kawaa highlights. Not an entitlement and not a price.

parameters.name: currency
parameters.description: Quote the packs in this currency: BRL, EUR, GBP, INR, USD. **Genuinely case-insensitive**: `isSupportedCurrency` upper-cases the value before checking it, so `usd`, `USD` and `Usd` are the same request. Expressed as a case-insensitive `pattern` rather than an `enum` on purpose: an enum can only list casings, and listing `USD` and `usd` still made a generated validator refuse `Usd`, which the API accepts. The response echoes the code lower-case. Anything else is 400.

get.description: Returns retained schedules for the authenticated account. scheduling_available and manual_run_available state whether this account can create, change and run schedules, and request a run now; an account without access can still read and remove retained schedules. Scheduled exports deliver by email, webhook or Amazon S3. Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage delivery is not available yet: a schedule that would deliver to one cannot be created, changed, resumed or run, and a run that reaches one fails without sending anything. run_in_progress means the schedule has an unfinished export request. Private credentials and run identities are omitted.

200.description: Owned schedules and current account availability.

post.summary: Request one export from an owned schedule
post.description: Available only when the account reports manual_run_available: true. Queues one export for the private worker; acceptance does not mean processing or delivery has completed. A one-off request can use a paused schedule and does not advance its recurring calendar. Both the schedule credential and requester must remain authorized for the selected data. Use one printable ASCII Idempotency-Key without spaces or commas, and reuse it after any uncertain response. A retry returns the original request, including its recorded failed or completed status. It never applies later schedule edits to the accepted request. An active schedule request prevents a second request until its final result. The replay receipt stays while work is unresolved and, after completion, for at least 30 days or the accepted output retention period, whichever is longer. A retained receipt whose completed output has been removed, is being deleted, or has expired returns 410 without restarting it. After the receipt itself expires, a request may be new; keep retries within 30 days of submission or deliberately start a new request. No verification credits are spent by this request. Completed means accepted by the delivery provider, not confirmed receipt in a mailbox.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: One token per requested export; reuse on retries. Do not contain commas or spaces.

200.description: Accepted request or the result of the same earlier request.

400.description: Invalid or missing request key, or saved schedule settings need correction.

403.description: The requester or originating schedule credential lacks current permission.

404.description: No owned schedule matches this identifier.

409.description: The schedule or permission changed, a run is active, or this key belongs to another requester. Retry the same key after checking the schedule.

410.description: IDEMPOTENT_EXPORT_EXPIRED: the accepted output is no longer retained; this retry did not start another export. Use a new key for a new request.

503.description: SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE with retryable: false. Scheduling or manual runs are not available to this account, or the schedule delivers to cloud storage on a provider that is not available yet (Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage).

ApiKeyHeader.name: X-Api-Key
ApiKeyHeader.description: A Kawaa API key, created in Settings → API keys. Format: `ev_` followed by 32 alphanumeric characters.

BearerToken.description: The same API key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Accepted everywhere `X-Api-Key` is. This scheme is the `ev_` API key only. An OAuth access token (`evo_` followed by 40 alphanumeric characters) travels in the same header, but it is the `OAuth2` scheme: it is always scoped, and it is accepted only by the operations that list `OAuth2`, with the scopes they name. An operation that lists `BearerToken` without `OAuth2` refuses it.

OAuth2.description:
OAuth 2.1 sign-in, for an app or agent that acts for a person who approves it on a Kawaa consent screen, instead of being handed an API key. The access token is sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, the same header as `BearerToken`, and is checked exactly like a scoped API key: scopes, rate limits and credits apply unchanged.

- **Discovery.** Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414): `https://api.kawaa.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`. Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728): `https://api.kawaa.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` for this API and `https://api.kawaa.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp` for the MCP server.
- **Client.** Use the https URL of a Client ID Metadata Document, on the default port, as `client_id` (public clients only), or register at `https://api.kawaa.com/oauth/register` (RFC 7591; no credential needed). Registration follows the RFC defaults when a field is omitted: `token_endpoint_auth_method` `client_secret_basic` (a secret is issued) and `grant_types` `authorization_code` alone. Send `none` for a public client, and include `refresh_token` in `grant_types` to be issued refresh tokens. A redirect URI is https, loopback http (any port), or an app's own scheme: a reversed domain name (RFC 8252 §7.1, `com.example.app:/callback`) or one of `cursor`, `vscode`, `vscode-insiders`, `claude` and `windsurf`. Browser and operating-system handler schemes are refused (`invalid_redirect_uri`).
- **PKCE.** Required on every authorization request, with `code_challenge_method=S256`; no other method is accepted. The only grants are `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`.
- **Resource.** Send `resource=https://api.kawaa.com` for this API (RFC 8707). Without it the token is issued for the MCP server, `https://api.kawaa.com/mcp`; any other value is refused with `invalid_target`.
- **Scopes.** With no `scope` parameter the request is for `verification:write verification:read account:read analytics:read`. Scopes Kawaa does not define, and scopes a connected app can never hold, are dropped rather than refused; if none remain the request is refused with `invalid_scope`. An authorization request refused before the person answers it (`invalid_request`, `unsupported_response_type`, `invalid_target`, `invalid_scope`) is shown to them on a Kawaa error page carrying that code, and is not sent to the redirect URI (RFC 9700 §4.11.2); only their answer is, the code or `access_denied`, with `state` and `iss`. The person approving can untick any scope, and the token response's `scope` states what was granted. `account:write`, `account:delete`, `billing:write`, `team:write`, `security:write` and `white_label:write` are never granted, so the operations that need them do not list this scheme, and neither do those marked `x-kawaa-unscoped-only`. As for API keys, `<area>:write` also satisfies `<area>:read`.
- **Tokens.** An access token is `evo_` followed by 40 alphanumeric characters and lasts one hour (`expires_in: 3600`); after that the API answers 401 `OAUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED`. A refresh token is `evr_` followed by 48 alphanumeric characters and is never accepted as a bearer credential. Every refresh returns a new refresh token and retires the one presented. The one just used may be presented up to 5 more times within 60 seconds of its use (a lost response, or several refreshes sent at once) and gets a new one of its own each time; the first of those to be used retires the rest. Presenting it again after that, or presenting any older refresh token, is treated as theft and ends the connection: its refresh tokens and every live access token stop working. A refresh may ask for fewer scopes than the connection holds, never more. A connection that is not refreshed for 30 days ends. Revoke at `https://api.kawaa.com/oauth/revoke` (RFC 7009).

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description:
Makes a charging call safe to retry: a repeat under the same key replays the original outcome instead of buying the work again. **The window depends on the route**: the receipt behind it expires, and after that the same key is a new paid request. It is 30 days for a deliverability check, at least 30 days for a single find, 24 hours for an activity lookup, and 15 minutes for a bulk find. What a replay returns also differs: a batch replays its JOB, an activity lookup replays its RESULT. A different request under the same key is 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT, before any charge.

**How long a key stays safe differs per route, and for the verification routes it depends on the plan.** `POST /v1/verify`, `/v1/verify/batch` and `/v1/verify/file` keep their receipts for the job's data-retention period, never less than **30 days** (`idempotencyReceiptTtl(keyedChargeTtl(getRetentionTtlSeconds(plan), job))`, with `IDEMPOTENCY_RECEIPT_MIN_DAYS` = 30), so longer on plans that keep results longer. The job itself is kept only for the plan's data-retention period, which is 7 days on Free: a repeat that arrives after the job's retention period has ended but while its receipt is still live is refused with `410 IDEMPOTENT_JOB_EXPIRED` and charged nothing, rather than bought a second time; send a new key to run it again. Once the receipt expires the same key claims a fresh target and creates another paid job. `POST /v1/deliverability/check` keeps its receipt 30 days. `POST /v1/find` keeps its receipt at least 30 days and its stored address only for the plan's retention period; a repeat after the address expires but before the receipt does return `410 IDEMPOTENT_JOB_EXPIRED` without charging. The activity lookups keep receipts about 24 hours, and `POST /v1/find/bulk` 15 minutes. Without a key, `GET /v1/activity/{email}` and `GET /v1/activity/domain/{domain}` still answer an identical repeat from the same account free for 15 minutes after the lookup that was charged (`POST /v1/find/bulk` does the same for its content); a key buys a fresh read inside that window. An unkeyed `POST /v1/verify` that arrives while an identical one from the same account is still being verified (at most 15 minutes after its charge) joins it and is not charged; once that verification has its answer, a repeat is charged as usual. Only a key makes a later retry free.

Retry with the key you have rather than minting a new one. A key is not a refund (it prevents a second charge, it does not undo the first), but it stays good far longer than the shortest advertised retention suggests, and dropping one early is how a retry becomes a second paid job.

**The characters are checked after trimming.** `readIdempotencyKey` first applies `String.trim()` to the header; the resulting key must be 1-255 printable ASCII characters (`0x21`-`0x7e`) other than a comma, with no internal spaces or anything outside that range. Leading and trailing whitespace is accepted and is not part of the key. Because OpenAPI constraints apply to the raw header rather than the post-trim value, this schema deliberately has no `minLength`, `maxLength`, or `pattern`; those constraints would make generated clients reject values the API accepts. Invalid post-trim values get 400 before the route starts. A UUID is the obvious choice. Sending the header twice with different raw values is also a 400. A key may not contain a comma, because a header sent more than once reaches the API joined by commas; a comma is refused with the same 400, before anything is charged. A receipt claimed under a comma-bearing key before 2026-10-03 still replays for its window.

Limit.name: limit
Limit.description: Page size, 1 to 100. A malformed, fractional, zero, negative or larger value is a 400 rather than silently clamped. Every response echoes the page size it applied.

RequestId.description: The identifier for this request. Quote it to support.

RetryAfter.description: Seconds to wait before retrying. `error.retry_after_seconds` in the body carries the same number.

RateLimitReset.description: Unix time at which the window resets.

ErrorEnvelope.description: Every failure is `{ "success": false, "error": { … } }`. Branch on `error.code`, not on the message. The retry fields are optional and are left out, never guessed, when the server does not know: `retryable` says whether repeating the identical request can succeed, `retry_after_seconds` how long to wait, and on a 5xx (or a refusal decided after the charge) from a route that charges credits one of `retry_requires_same_idempotency_key` or `retry_may_charge_again` says how to repeat it without paying twice.

retryable.description: Whether the identical request, sent again after a wait with nothing else changed, can succeed. `true` for rate limiting and transient failures; `false` when the request, the credential, the plan, the balance or the resource has to change first. Absent when the answer depends on the case, notably `INTERNAL_ERROR` (an unexpected failure, transient or not) and `CONFLICT`. Decided per code; a few responses override their code, such as a `503` for a feature switched off in this deployment (`false`) or a `400` for a download whose job is still running (`true`).

retry_after_seconds.description: Seconds to wait before retrying, when the server knows. The same number as the `Retry-After` header, which is sent with it.

retry_requires_same_idempotency_key.description: Present on a 5xx from a route that charges credits and honours `Idempotency-Key`, for a request that sent one. Repeat it only with the same `Idempotency-Key`: an attempt under the key that was charged is replayed rather than bought again, for as long as the key's receipt lasts, and one that was not is simply run. An instruction, not a claim that this attempt was charged.

nothing_charged.description: Present only when the server can confirm that this attempt left no charge standing: it failed before the debit, the debit did not commit, or the charge was refunded. It does not describe earlier attempts under the same request key. Continue to reuse the same Idempotency-Key when instructed. Absence does not establish whether a charge occurred.

retry_may_charge_again.description: Present on a 5xx (or a refusal decided after the charge, such as an AI-provider 429 once a composition was paid for) from a route that charges credits, for a request with no `Idempotency-Key` to reuse (the route takes none, or the caller sent none), when the server cannot rule out that this attempt was charged. No key marks a repeat as the same request (some routes forgive an identical repeat for a short window, none promises to), so a retry may be charged a second time. Check `GET /v1/usage/credits/transactions`, which lists each debit with its timestamp and description, to see whether this attempt was charged; `GET /v1/usage` gives the balance but not the per-debit detail that answers the question.

granted_scopes.description: Present on an `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` sent to an app connected over OAuth: the scopes its access token holds. To ask for the missing scope it signs in again requesting these together with the scopes the message names; some clients (Codex CLI's `--scopes`) replace their whole request with the list they are given.

ErrorCode.description: The machine-readable reason. NOT a closed set: handlers add codes, and a client that refuses an unfamiliar one rejects ordinary API errors instead of handling them. Branch on the codes you know and fall back to the HTTP status. `examples` lists every code this build's handlers can return in an error envelope, whether passed to `error(...)` or written into a response body as `{code, message}`, including some from routes this document does not describe, because a client can still meet them. `TEAM_DELETION_IN_PROGRESS` is the odd one: it arrives with `202`, on a deletion that is proceeding rather than failing.

VerificationStatus.description: The verdict. `catch_all` means the domain accepts mail for every recipient, so this particular mailbox could not be checked: it is neither a yes nor a no. `unknown` means the check could not conclude.

SubStatus.description: Why the verdict came out as it did. New values can be added without a version change; treat an unfamiliar one as informational. Deliberately NOT a closed enum: the list above is what this build emits, and a new reason ships without a version bump. A generated validator built from a closed set would reject an otherwise valid verification result the day one is added, which is the opposite of the forward compatibility this field promises.

VerifyOptions.description: Only these option names are accepted. Anything else is a 400 naming the supported ones, rather than being ignored while the response reads as applied. Omit `options` to use the defaults. A present `null` is a wrong-type value and is refused with `400 INVALID_OPTION` before anything is verified or charged.

deep_verify.description: Attempt an SMTP conversation with the receiving server.

include_ai.description: Run the AI-assisted checks (default `true`). Turning it off does more than remove AI analysis. The built-in rules alone then answer the typo and catch-all checks, so `ai` and `suggestion` still appear when they find something. The worker also skips the SPF, DKIM and DMARC lookup, which runs only with this option on: `domain_info` then carries `auth_score`, `auth_grade`, `has_spf`, `spf_policy`, `has_dmarc`, `dmarc_policy` and `has_dkim` only when a recent check of the same domain already measured them, so expect them to be absent.

enrich.description: Include name, gender and country hints where available. Needs the Business plan or higher: on a lower plan the whole request is refused with `403 PLAN_UPGRADE_REQUIRED` and nothing is charged.

skip_cache.description: Ignore a cached result and verify fresh. Charges the full rate.

timeout_ms.description:
How long `POST /v1/verify` waits (whole milliseconds) for a verdict before answering `status: "pending"`. **Normalized, not honoured verbatim**, and normalized rather than refused: the default is 24,000 ms, a positive value below 5,000 is raised to 5,000, and anything above 25,000 is capped at 25,000: asking for 60,000 gets `pending` after about 25 seconds. Zero and negative numbers fall back to the default. The cap can fall further on a request that has already spent time on auth and credits, because polling must finish inside the gateway's 29-second integration timeout.

No `minimum` or `maximum` is declared here on purpose: they would make a generated client refuse locally what the API accepts and clamps. A present value that is not a whole number is the one case that IS refused, with `400 INVALID_OPTION`: nothing is verified and nothing is charged. That includes a fraction such as `7500.5`: the verification worker reads this field as an unsigned integer, and a fractional value used to be charged for and then dropped as an unreadable job.

A pending answer is not a failure: poll `GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}`.

email.description: The address to verify. **Normalized before it is validated**, so this is deliberately not constrained with `format: email`: `normalizeEmail` trims surrounding whitespace, lower-cases the address and punycodes an internationalized domain, and only then does `isValidEmail` run. So `" User@Example.com "` and `user@münchen.de` are both accepted and are charged like any other address, while a strict email-format validator would refuse the raw strings. The response echoes the NORMALIZED form, so compare against that, not against what you sent.

include_activity.description: Attach your own account's engagement history for the address as `activity`. `domain_reputation` is reserved and not sent today, because Kawaa stores no domain reputation score. Adds NO charge of its own: the call debits once (1 credit fresh, 0.5 from cache) whether or not you ask for it.

items.description: Not constrained to a valid address on purpose: the endpoint removes malformed entries and reports how many in `invalid_emails_skipped`, which is a supported way to clean a list. Validating them away here would refuse requests the API accepts.

emails.description: The addresses to verify. `maxItems` here is the ABSOLUTE ceiling (Enterprise); the limit that applies is your plan's (Free 100, Starter 1,000, Professional and Business 5,000, Enterprise 10,000), and a longer list is **413** `BATCH_SIZE_EXCEEDED` before anything is charged: a capacity refusal, not malformed input, so an integration can branch on the status and split or upgrade rather than treating it as a bad request. `GET /v1/account` reports the plan. At least one entry must be a usable address; a list with none is a 400.

webhook_url.description: Where to POST the completion callback. HTTPS only: `validateWebhookUrl` refuses anything else with 400 WEBHOOK_URL_INVALID. Without a `webhook_secret` the callback is unsigned. Omit the field for no callback; an explicit `null` is a wrong-type value and is refused before the job is created or charged. No scheme `pattern` is declared: `validateWebhookUrlStatic` parses with `new URL()`, which tolerates surrounding whitespace and normalizes the protocol, so `" https://x"` and `"HTTPS://x"` are both accepted, and an anchored lower-case pattern refused both. It must still be HTTPS; that is checked on the parsed protocol, not on the string you sent.

webhook_secret.description: Signs the callback to `webhook_url`. Stored with the job, and every delivery then carries `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` (an HMAC of the send time and the body, which lets you refuse a replay) and the legacy `X-Kawaa-Signature` computed from it. The flat callback body has no timestamp of its own, so check the `t` in `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2`. Without it the callback is UNSIGNED and anything that can reach your URL can post a convincing completion. Only meaningful alongside `webhook_url`. It has no meaning on its own: a secret with no `webhook_url` is 400 `INVALID_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, because there is no callback to sign. `dependentRequired` says so above. Omit the field for unsigned callbacks; an explicit `null` is refused with `400 INVALID_WEBHOOK_SECRET` before the job is created or charged.

filename.description: The name to store the upload under. **Measured after trimming**: `requireStringField` trims the value before checking its length and the extension, so `" report.csv "` is accepted and stored as `report.csv`. No `pattern` or `maxLength` is declared here for that reason: an end-anchored pattern and a raw length check both refuse values this route accepts. The trimmed name must be 1-255 characters and end in `.csv`, `.tsv` or `.txt`; `.csv` on its own is a name the handler serves.

file_size.description: The size of the file in bytes, as it will be uploaded. The upload URL is signed for exactly this many bytes, so S3 refuses a body of any other length (`403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`); ask for a new URL if the file changes. Required: a missing, `null`, fractional or non-positive value is `400`, and a file over 50 MB (52,428,800 bytes) is `413 BATCH_SIZE_EXCEEDED` before any upload.

file_key.description: The key returned by `get_upload_url`. The TRIMMED value must be 1-1,024 characters and must sit under your own upload prefix. **Measured after trimming.** `requireStringField` / `optionalStringField` trim the value before checking its length, so no length bound is declared on the raw string here: a raw `maxLength` refuses a valid value padded with spaces, and a raw `minLength` accepts a whitespace-only one the route then rejects with 400.

webhook_url.description:
Where to POST the completion callback. The TRIMMED value must be at most 2,048 characters and must use HTTPS. **Measured after trimming.** `requireStringField` / `optionalStringField` trim the value before checking its length, so no length bound is declared on the raw string here: a raw `maxLength` refuses a valid value padded with spaces, and a raw `minLength` accepts a whitespace-only one the route then rejects with 400. HTTPS only: `validateWebhookUrl` refuses anything else with 400 WEBHOOK_URL_INVALID. Omit the field for no callback; an explicit `null` is refused with 400 before the file is read or credits are charged.

Without a `webhook_secret` the callback is unsigned. No `format: uri` or anchored scheme `pattern` is declared on this REQUEST field: `validateWebhookUrlStatic` parses with `new URL()`, which tolerates surrounding whitespace and normalizes the protocol, so `" https://x"` and `"HTTPS://x"` are both accepted while either constraint refuses them. HTTPS is required, checked on the PARSED protocol, not on the string you sent. The response fields keep `format: uri`, because what the server hands back really is a well-formed URI.

webhook_secret.description: Signs the callback to `webhook_url`, as on `POST /v1/verify/batch`. Stored with the job, and every delivery then carries `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` (an HMAC of the send time and the body, which lets you refuse a replay) and the legacy `X-Kawaa-Signature` computed from it. Without it the callback is UNSIGNED and anything that can reach your URL can post a convincing completion. A secret with no `webhook_url` is 400 `INVALID_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, because there is no callback to sign; `dependentRequired` says so above. Omit the field for unsigned callbacks; an explicit `null` is refused with `400 INVALID_WEBHOOK_SECRET` before the file is read or credits are charged. Part of the request an `Idempotency-Key` identifies: the same key with a different secret is `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT`.

first_name.description: Must contain at least one letter AFTER normalization, which spells the name in a-z: accents are dropped and letters such as `ø`, `æ`, `ß`, `ł` and `þ` are written `o`, `ae`, `ss`, `l` and `th`; then only `a-z` is kept. `José`, `Ñuñez` and `Søren` are fine, `李`, `2024` and `!!` are not. A name that normalizes to nothing generates no candidate addresses, so the API answers `400 first_name and last_name must contain letters (a-z)` and charges nothing. A name with a letter that has no single a-z spelling (such as `ə` or `ʒ`) next to letters that do is also a 400 that charges nothing, and so is one that spells to more than 64 letters. Deliberately not a `pattern` here: the check runs on the normalized form, and a regex over the raw string would refuse names this API accepts.

last_name.description: Must contain at least one letter AFTER normalization, which spells the name in a-z: accents are dropped and letters such as `ø`, `æ`, `ß`, `ł` and `þ` are written `o`, `ae`, `ss`, `l` and `th`; then only `a-z` is kept. `José`, `Ñuñez` and `Søren` are fine, `李`, `2024` and `!!` are not. A name that normalizes to nothing generates no candidate addresses, so the API answers `400 first_name and last_name must contain letters (a-z)` and charges nothing. A name with a letter that has no single a-z spelling (such as `ə` or `ʒ`) next to letters that do is also a 400 that charges nothing, and so is one that spells to more than 64 letters. Deliberately not a `pattern` here: the check runs on the normalized form, and a regex over the raw string would refuse names this API accepts.

domain.description: The company's mail domain, as a bare name. A special-use name (`.example`, `.test`, `.invalid`, `.localhost`, `.local`, `.onion`, `.alt`, `.internal`, `.corp`, `.home`, `.mail`, `home.arpa` and the other special-use `.arpa` names) and RFC 2606's `example.com` / `.net` / `.org` with any name under them are a 400 before the charge: no mailbox can exist there. So are a domain that cannot receive mail (no such domain, a null MX, or neither an MX nor an address record) and a public mailbox provider such as gmail.com.

The company's mail domain, as a bare name. A special-use name (`.example`, `.test`, `.invalid`, `.localhost`, `.local`, `.onion`, `.alt`, `.internal`, `.corp`, `.home`, `.mail`, `home.arpa` and the other special-use `.arpa` names) and RFC 2606's `example.com` / `.net` / `.org` with any name under them are a 400 before the charge: no mailbox can exist there.

people.description: Up to 50 people per request; more is a 400 before any lookup or charge.

batch_job_id.description: The batch or file job this result belongs to, when it belongs to one: on a batch row of `GET /v1/jobs/{id}` it is the same id as `job_id`. Omitted from a single verification (`POST /v1/verify`, and its job read back through `GET /v1/jobs/{id}`), which belongs to no batch.

catch_all.description: The domain accepts mail for any address, so an accepted mailbox proves nothing on its own. Omitted when the catch-all probe did not measure it: the check ended before any probe (a disposable or spam-trap verdict, a domain with no usable mail server), the mail server refused or never answered for the mailbox so the probe never ran, or the probe could not settle it (that result is `risky`). Also `true` beside `provider_accept_all`, where the mail provider accepts addresses it does not have. Absent is not `false`.

mailbox_exists.description: `true` when the mail server accepted the mailbox at RCPT TO, on a domain that does not accept every address. `false` when the server answered RCPT TO without accepting it: read it as "not confirmed", not "confirmed absent". It is usually a refusal of the mailbox (`status: "invalid"`), but it is also `false` when the answer was temporary (`status: "unknown"`, `sub_status` `greylisted` or `temporary_failure`) or the server refused the sender rather than the mailbox (`sub_status: "policy_block"`), so read it with `status` and `sub_status`. Omitted when no server answered RCPT TO (no probe ran, the connection failed, or the conversation was refused before RCPT, for example at the greeting), when an acceptance proves nothing (`catch_all`, `provider_accept_all` or a `risky` result), and when the server said the mailbox is full. Absent is not `false`.

provider_accept_all.description: The PROVIDER accepts recipient probes too broadly for an individual mailbox to be confirmed. Not the same as `catch_all`, which is the domain's own configuration. Present when the worker could tell. SMTP acceptance here is not evidence the mailbox exists, and a client that treats it as such publishes a deliverability claim nothing measured.

flags.description: Independent of the verdict: an address can be valid and also role_account.

abuse_email.description: The local part matched an abuse, complaint-handling, feedback-loop, legal or blocklist-removal name or pattern, at any domain, such as abuse@, postmaster@, feedback@, legal@, spam-alerts@ or abuse1@. Every address with complainer set has it too. With AI analysis on, the model can also raise it for a local part containing abuse, spam or complaint. A match on the address itself, not a finding about what the mailbox is used for or anything its owner has done.

complainer.description: A narrower abuse_email: the address is a complaint-handling mailbox, such as abuse@, postmaster@, fbl@ or feedback@, at a reviewed anti-spam, feedback-loop, sender-reputation or consumer-protection organization, such as spamhaus.org, spamcop.net or ftc.gov. The same local part at any other domain, and any other mailbox at those organizations, does not raise it. A match on the address itself, not complaint history: verification does not derive it from any record of who has marked mail as spam.

domain_info.description: The domain's provider type and email-authentication posture. The SPF, DKIM and DMARC fields (`auth_score`, `auth_grade`, `has_spf`, `spf_policy`, `has_dmarc`, `dmarc_policy`, `has_dkim`) are each omitted when their lookup failed or did not run. The lookup runs only when `options.include_ai` is on (the default); with it off, they are present only when a recent check of the same domain already measured them.

typo_suggestion.description: A corrected address when one looks likely; omitted when there is none. The same value as the top-level `suggestion`. This is the field the worker serializes; there is no `suggested_email`.

typo_confidence.description: How confident the correction is, when one was made.

typo_method.description: How the suggestion was arrived at, as the detector names it. Present whenever `typo_suggestion` is. Treat it as an open set: it is the detector's own label, and a new detector adds a new one.

catch_all_confidence.description: 0-100, and only for a domain that accepts everything: how likely this particular mailbox is real despite the catch-all. It is the one piece of evidence that separates two `catch_all` addresses, and it is absent on every other result.

ai.description: Present when the worker has something to report: it is built when there is a typo suggestion or a catch-all confidence, and omitted otherwise. That holds whether or not `include_ai` is set: without it the built-in rules produce both; with it, AI analysis is tried first and the rules are the fallback. The four fields below are every field it can carry: `fraud_score` and `patterns` exist in the worker's struct but are never populated, so they never appear.

suggestion.description:
The corrected address when the domain looks like a misspelling of a well-known one, such as `jane@gmail.com` for `jane@gmial.com`. The same value as `ai.typo_suggestion`, and present exactly when that is. It is advice only: `status` and every check describe the address that was sent, not the correction.

The typo check runs whether or not `include_ai` is set; with it, AI analysis can also catch misspellings the built-in list does not. Omitted (never `null`) when there is no correction.

idempotent_replay.description: `POST /v1/verify` only. True when this request, sent without an `Idempotency-Key`, joined an identical request whose verification was still in flight and was answered from it: `credits_used` is `0` and nothing was charged. Absent when this request paid for the verdict.

activity.description: Engagement history, attached only when the request asked for it with `include_activity`. Read from your own account's tracking only, never another account's. When your tracking has recorded nothing for the address it is still an object, with `level: "unknown"`, `score: 0`, `last_activity_at: null`, zero counts and `data_points: 0`; that is not a signal about the mailbox. Absent when the request did not ask for it, and when the activity could not be read.

domain_reputation.description: Reserved for a stored numeric domain reputation score when `include_activity` is true. Kawaa does not compute one today, so current responses omit this field.

enrichment.description: Attached when the request set `options.enrich` and the plan includes data enrichment. Null when nothing is known, which is not a judgement about the address.

cache_age_seconds.description: How old the cached result is, in seconds. Present on every cache hit, beside `from_cache: true`. Without it a result reused from days ago reads exactly like one measured this second.

classifier_version.description: Which verdict classifier produced this result. Stamped by the worker onto every newly produced result. When the classifier changes a cached result from an older version is never reused (the address is verified afresh), so two results with different values here were not decided by the same rules.

PendingVerification.description: No verdict yet. Not a result: poll the job.

credits_held.description: Held, not spent. Refunded by reconciliation if the worker never produces a result. Absent on a request that joined an identical one still in flight (`idempotent_replay: true`): that request holds nothing.

activity.description: Engagement history, attached only when the request asked for it with `include_activity`. Read from your own account's tracking only, never another account's. When your tracking has recorded nothing for the address it is still an object, with `level: "unknown"`, `score: 0`, `last_activity_at: null`, zero counts and `data_points: 0`; that is not a signal about the mailbox. Absent when the request did not ask for it, and when the activity could not be read.
