credits_used.description: What this call charged. Present on a pending result too: the debit happens before the verdict does. `0` on a request that joined an identical one still in flight (`idempotent_replay: true`).

idempotent_replay.description: True when this repeated an earlier `POST /v1/verify` under the same `Idempotency-Key`, or, without a key, joined an identical request whose verification was still in flight: the job is the ORIGINAL one and nothing more was charged. **Absent means this request created the job**: the handler adds the field only on a replay. `credits_used: 0` accompanies it, which on its own is ambiguous because a pending answer can also report held rather than spent credits; this is the field that says which. Poll `GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}` either way.

request_id.description: Identifier of this API request. Quote it when contacting support.

BatchAccepted.description: What `POST /v1/verify/batch` answers with on acceptance. `unique_emails` is what the job will verify; `credits_used` is what was charged, and the two can differ when SQS delivery is ambiguous; see the fields themselves.

unique_emails.description: Addresses CONFIRMED queued: what the job will actually verify. It is not always what was charged: when SQS delivery is ambiguous the handler confirms what it can and reports the rest in `enqueue_unknown`, so this can be lower than `credits_used` and, in the extreme, 0 on a job that charged. Reconcile billing against `credits_used` and `credits_held`, never against this count.

duplicates_removed.description: Removed before charging: the same address twice costs once.

invalid_emails_skipped.description: Rejected as malformed and never verified. The results will be shorter than the list you sent.

credits_remaining.description: Absent when the post-charge balance could not be safely recovered.

idempotent_replay.description: True when this returned an earlier submission's job and charged nothing.

dispatch_in_progress.description: A request under this same `Idempotency-Key` is still queueing the batch. Nothing more was charged. Retry after `Retry-After`, or poll the job.

enqueue_unknown.description: How many sends could not be confirmed. Credits for them are HELD, not spent. Poll the job until it reconciles.

credits_held.description: Held pending reconciliation of an ambiguous enqueue. Not a settled charge.

estimated_time_seconds.description: A rough estimate of how long the job will take, at about two seconds per address. An estimate for a progress bar, not a deadline. Poll `GET /v1/jobs/{job_id}` for the truth.

enqueue_failures.description: How many addresses SQS DEFINITIVELY rejected, present only when some were. Distinct from `enqueue_unknown`, which is "we do not know". Their credits are refunded where the refund succeeds; where it does not they stay held and `message` says so, so this number beside an unchanged `credits_used` is the case to reconcile rather than to retry.

JobSummary.description: Four buckets, and they are BUCKETS rather than verdicts. `summaryForStatus` in `lambda/job-status/index.ts` is the whole rule: `valid` is exactly `valid`; `invalid` is `invalid` AND `disposable`; `risky` is `risky`, `catch_all`, `role` and `spam_trap`; `unknown` is `unknown` and any row with no stored status. A per-address verdict is in the result row, not here, and `catch_all` inside `risky` is the one worth remembering, because it is inconclusive rather than bad.

invalid.description: Rows whose verdict is `invalid` OR `disposable`. Building a suppression list from this bucket therefore removes disposable addresses too, which is usually intended.

risky.description: Rows whose verdict is `risky`, `catch_all`, `role` or `spam_trap`. Mixed: `catch_all` is inconclusive, not bad.

unknown.description: Rows whose verdict is `unknown`, plus any row with no stored status at all.

status.description:
The job's state. `enqueue_unknown` means some sends could not be confirmed and credits are held pending reconciliation. Poll until it resolves.

**`cancelled` is what `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel` produces.** Stopping a batch leaves the addresses already checked in place, billed, and readable; the credits held for the rest are refunded. Because the refund waits for in-flight addresses to finish, a job can read `cancelled` with `billing_status: "charged"` for a few minutes before it reads `refunded`. That is the refund draining, not a failure, and nothing is required of you.

**Cancelled or not, handle it as terminal, and do so immediately.** A cancelled job's verdicts are final the moment the status says so: every result is written together with the job's progress counter in one conditional write requiring the job to still be running, so the cancel closes the result set as it lands. What is NOT final yet is the bill: the refund for the addresses it never checked waits for the in-flight ones to time out. That is what `completed_at` marks, and the repository SDKs expose it as `isSettled` / `is_settled`. Read it if you are reconciling the charge; do not make your results wait on it. What must not happen is treating `cancelled` as still-running and polling for ever.

Terminal does NOT mean empty: such a job can carry a **partial** result set, and `GET /v1/jobs/{id}?include_results=true` returns it: the handler gates on `processed_emails > 0`, not on status, so the addresses it did check come back. Read `processed_emails` against `total_emails` to see how far it got, and do not discard those results. `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/download` exports exactly those addresses too. Read progress as `processed_emails` of `requested_emails`: a job that stopped early has `total_emails` collapsed onto what it actually checked and billed.

**A cancel is a brake, not a substitute for sizing the batch.** The submission-time limits still apply and still refuse first: the plan's per-batch ceiling (`413 BATCH_SIZE_EXCEEDED`), the 10,000 global cap, and the credit balance (`402`). Cancelling after the fact returns the unprocessed credits, never the ones already spent.

cache_discount_pending.description: Present, and only ever `true`, when this read tried to apply the per-address cache discount and could not, almost always because the results index had not caught up, so the cached count could not be trusted yet. The next read retries it. It exists because nothing else on the job tells "checked, nothing owed" apart from "could not check": both leave a `completed` or `cancelled` job's credits unchanged. If you are reconciling the charge, you have one more read to do while this is true.

requested_emails.description: The list size you submitted. Present only when some of it will never have a result: a job that was cancelled or stopped early, or one where some addresses could not be queued when you submitted it or never came back from the queue. `total_emails` is then lowered to the addresses actually checked and billed, and the rest are refunded. That is how the platform records that the job owes nothing more for them. Read progress as `processed_emails` of this. The same figure as `requested_emails` on the `job.completed` webhook.

partial.description: Present, and only ever `true`, exactly when `requested_emails` is: `requested_emails` minus `total_emails` addresses have no result and never will, and their credits were refunded. A `completed` job can carry it. The same signal as `partial` on the `job.completed` webhook, so polling this endpoint after a missed delivery tells you what the delivery would have. Absent while `total_emails` still counts every address you submitted: a cancelled job gains it when the refund for the addresses it never checked is applied, which `completed_at` marks.

file_counts.description: What the uploaded file held, as `POST /v1/verify/file` counted it when it created the job: the same four figures its acceptance response reported, under the same names. Present on the single job, as `GET /v1/jobs/{id}` and `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel` return it, when the job was created from a file; never on the listing, and absent on a job submitted as a list and on a file job recorded before these counts were stored. `total_emails` is only the addresses verified, so this is the one place the rows that were skipped or merged are still accounted for. `total_submitted` = `unique_emails` + `duplicates_removed` + `invalid_emails_skipped`.

total_submitted.description: Rows read from the file, including the invalid ones. A header row is not counted.

invalid_emails_skipped.description: Rows that were not addresses. Skipped, not charged for, and not in the job.

duplicates_removed.description: Repeats of an earlier address (compared case-insensitively). Removed before charging.

unique_emails.description: Distinct addresses the file yielded: what the job was created to verify.

next_key.description: Cursor for the next page of results.

completed_at.description: When the job's books closed for the CANCELLATION refund. Null while the job is running and (on a `cancelled` one) until the refund for the unprocessed addresses commits, or the platform settles a job that owed nothing. It says nothing about the results, which are final as soon as the status is terminal. It is not the whole bill either: an ordinary `completed` batch has this set and can still owe its per-address cache discount, and so can a `cancelled` one (its discount on the addresses it did check is applied right after this refund), which `cache_discount_pending` reports. Reconciling a charge means reading both.

cancelled_at.description: When `POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel` stopped the job. Absent on every other job.

error_message.description: Why a terminal job ended as it did, in Kawaa's own customer-safe words, present on failures and on reconciliation outcomes. Without it, `status: "failed"` is the whole story a client can tell.

jobs.description: Each row is a `Job` plus `filename`, which is how a file upload is told from a submitted list. The per-job endpoint does not carry it.

limit.description: The page size that was applied.

total.description: Every job matching the listing, not just this page.

total_is_approximate.description: True when the count stopped at its scan bound, so `total` is a floor.

level.description: How recently this address was seen active. `inactive` sits between the active and dormant windows; `unknown` means there was nothing to judge from, not that the address is inactive.

reply_count.description: Counts replies recorded by Kawaa email warmup campaigns only. It is not a measurement of replies to your own mail, which Kawaa cannot see. Warmup is switched off, so no new replies are recorded, and new opens and clicks come only from your own tracking pixels and links.

confidence.description: 0 means your account has recorded no activity for this address, not that it is inactive.

message.description: Present only when no activity data is available for a single-address lookup.

email.description: The validated address, echoed unchanged from the path. Malformed or whitespace-padded values are refused before the paid lookup begins.

credits_remaining.description: The account's balance after this call. On a charged lookup, the balance the charge left. On a replay (`idempotent_replay: true`), the current balance as read when the replay authenticated, or, for a copy racing the charge, the lower of that and what the charge left. Absent when the balance could not be read.

idempotent_replay.description: True when this repeated an earlier lookup and therefore charged nothing: one under the same `Idempotency-Key` (that receipt lasts about 24 hours), or, without a key, the same address looked up by the same account within 15 minutes of the lookup that was charged. **Absent means it was charged**: `activityReceiptResponse` adds the field only on a replay. `credits_used: 0` alone cannot tell you which happened, because a lookup with nothing to bill also reports 0; this is the field that distinguishes them.

sendingIp.description: The `sending_ip` this check ran against, or null when none was supplied. Part of the raw scoring result, published alongside the snake_case projection in its original camelCase spelling; kept because existing integrations read it.

score.description: 0-100, over the mechanisms that were measured. One whose lookup failed is left out rather than scored as missing, so read `not_measured` before treating this as the whole picture. When `grade` is null, SPF, DKIM or DMARC was not measured and this is a partial score over what did answer: report it as partial, not as the domain's result.

grade.description: `score` as a letter: A (90-100), B (80-89), C (70-79), D (60-69) or F. **null when SPF, DKIM or DMARC could not be looked up** (named in `not_measured`): a letter over the rest would grade records nobody read, and it used to, so a domain whose DKIM and DMARC lookups both failed could read A. A stored check from before this rule that carries such a letter is answered with null too, from its own `not_measured`. A failed MX or reverse-DNS lookup still leaves a grade, over the rest; see `not_measured`.

checkedAt.description: When the check ran, as recorded in the raw scoring result. Prefer `checked_at`: on a cached or replayed result the stored row's `checked_at` is authoritative, and an older stored result may carry no `checkedAt` at all.

durationMs.description: How long the DNS work took, in milliseconds, for the run that produced this result. A cached or replayed answer repeats the original run's figure; it is not the latency of this request.

checks.description:
The raw per-mechanism scoring detail. One entry per mechanism REPORTED, and they do NOT share a shape: `dkim` carries the selectors it found, `mx` the records, `blacklists` the zones and the listings, and `mx` and `ptr` carry no `issues` array at all. Read the named property, not a common map value.

**Optional, and absent on an older stored result.** `projectDeliverabilityResult` tolerates a row with no `checks` bag (`internal.checks ?? {}`) and does not synthesize one, so a check stored before the current shape answers 200 with the projected fields and no `checks`. Read `authentication`, `dns`, `reputation` and `server`, which the projection always produces, and treat this as the raw detail when it happens to be there.

**BIMI and MTA-STS are checked, and they are unscored.** Both initialise `maxScore: 0`, and the scoring loop counts a mechanism only when `maxScore > 0`, so neither can move `score` or `grade` in either direction. They also have no entry in this object. A missing MTA-STS raises nothing at all; a missing BIMI produces a recommendation only when DMARC is already `reject`.

spf.description: SPF: whether a record exists, parses, and is not over the lookup limit.

status.description: `missing` is an answer: the name has no such record (NXDOMAIN or NODATA). `error` means the lookup itself failed (SERVFAIL, REFUSED, a timeout), so nothing is known about the record: the mechanism is not measured, has `maxScore` 0, is named in `not_measured` and is left out of the score; when it is SPF, DKIM or DMARC the check has no grade. `found`, `listed` and `skipped` are used by some mechanisms only.

score.description: What this mechanism contributed to the total, in raw points out of `maxScore`. The projected sections restate the same measurement as a percentage: `authentication.<mechanism>.score`, `dns.mx_score` and `reputation.score` are `round(score / maxScore × 100)`, so `checks.dkim` at 11 of 15 appears as `authentication.dkim.score: 73`. Two scales, one measurement.

maxScore.description: The most it could have contributed. A mechanism whose lookup failed (status `error`, named in `not_measured`) has `maxScore` 0 and is left out of the grade rather than scored as missing, the way an unanswered blocklist section is. For SPF, DKIM or DMARC there is then no grade at all (`grade: null`). Until 2026-10-01 a failed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MX or PTR lookup scored 0 against its full weight, so a DKIM SERVFAIL took a perfect domain from 100 (A) to 81 (B).

severity.description: How serious the finding is. `error` is what a missing SPF, DMARC, MX or PTR record produces, the common case on a paid check. A lookup that failed is a `warning` saying the mechanism was not measured, never an `error`.

A mechanism whose lookup failed (status `error`, named in `not_measured`) has `maxScore` 0 and is left out of the grade rather than scored as missing, the way an unanswered blocklist section is. For SPF, DKIM or DMARC there is then no grade at all (`grade: null`). Until 2026-10-01 a failed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MX or PTR lookup scored 0 against its full weight, so a DKIM SERVFAIL took a perfect domain from 100 (A) to 81 (B).

listed.description: The zones that answered "listed". Empty is the good case.

checked.description: Zones that gave a definitive answer either way.

inconclusive.description: Zones that were asked and answered nothing usable: a timeout, a refusal, a SERVFAIL. NOT a pass: an unanswered zone is not evidence of a clean record, and it contributes neither a pass nor its share of `maxScore`.

skipped.description: Zones that were never asked, e.g. IP zones when no `sending_ip` was given.

total.description: Zones in the list. `checked + inconclusive + skipped`.

severity.description: How serious the finding is. `error` is what a missing SPF, DMARC, MX or PTR record produces, the common case on a paid check. A lookup that failed is a `warning` saying the mechanism was not measured, never an `error`.

check_id.description: The saved check. Fetch it again with `GET /v1/deliverability/checks/{id}`: free, and the only way back to a result whose response was lost.

credits_used.description: What this call actually charged: 10 for a fresh check, 0 for a cached one or an idempotent replay. Read this rather than the price list.

credits_remaining.description: Balance after the charge. Omitted when it could not be read; its absence is not a zero balance.

cached.description: Present and true when this reused a check from the last 24 hours, which costs nothing. Send `refresh: true` to measure again.

idempotent_replay.description: Present and true when this returned an earlier call's result under the same `Idempotency-Key`, and charged nothing. Distinct from `cached`: a replay can return a FRESH check that was already paid for.

issues.description: Every finding, across every mechanism, severity-sorted. This is the list to render: the per-mechanism `issues` arrays do not carry MX, PTR or blocklist findings at all, so rebuilding this from `checks` loses exactly the problems that stop mail being delivered.

recommendations.description: What to change, in the order worth doing it. The remediation half of the 10 credits: a score with no recommendations is a grade without an answer. Empty on a domain with nothing to fix.

items.description: One thing to change, and how.

priority.description: Do the `high` ones first: they are the missing records that cause mail to be rejected outright, rather than the weak ones that cost reputation slowly.

category.description: Which part of the setup this is about, e.g. `Authentication`, `Reputation`, `Infrastructure`.

issue.description: What is wrong, in one line.

fix.description: What to change, concretely: usually the record to publish and roughly what to put in it.

not_measured.description: The scored mechanisms whose DNS lookup failed (SERVFAIL, REFUSED, a timeout), keyed by `spf`, `dkim`, `dmarc`, `mx` or `ptr`, each with a sentence saying why. Present only when at least one did; absent when every lookup answered, and on checks stored before 2026-10-01. A mechanism named here is unknown, not missing: its raw `checks.<mechanism>.status` is `error` with `maxScore` 0, its projected status is `not_measured`, it is left out of `score`, and it produces no recommendation. When it is `spf`, `dkim` or `dmarc`, `grade` and `spam_assessment.spam_likelihood` are null. The check is still charged, like any check that got real answers, with or without a grade; it is refunded (503) only when every lookup timed out or nothing at all could be scored. The 24-hour cache serves the stored result, so send `refresh: true` to measure again.

examples.dkim: DKIM lookup failed for 19 of 19 selectors (ESERVFAIL), so DKIM was not measured and is left out of the score.

checked_at.description: When the check ran. Falls back to the Unix epoch on an older cached row that stored none. A timestamp of `1970-01-01` means "not recorded", not "checked in 1970".

dns.description: The mail exchangers, as the projection reports them.

ip.description: Null unless the host was resolved during the check; usually null.

has_valid_mx.description: True only when the MX check passed AND at least one record came back. Also false when the MX lookup failed; `not_measured.mx` then says it was not measured rather than absent.

mx_score.description: The MX contribution, normalized to 100. 0 when the MX lookup failed, which `not_measured.mx` names; read it as unknown, not as no MX.

authentication.description: SPF, DKIM and DMARC as three comparable results. This is the half of the answer a sender acts on; `recommendations` says what to do about it.

status.description: The projection's status: `pass`, `fail`, `missing` or `not_measured`. `missing` means no record was found and is not the same as `fail`, which means one was found and did not hold up. `not_measured` means the lookup failed (SERVFAIL, REFUSED, a timeout), so nothing is known about the record; it is named in `not_measured` with the reason, left out of `score`, and the check has no `grade`. Added 2026-10-01: before then such a lookup read `missing`. A stored check from before then never carries it.

record.description: The published record, or null when none was found.

score.description: This mechanism's contribution, already normalized to 100: `round(checks.spf.score / checks.spf.maxScore × 100)`, 0 when nothing could be scored, including when it was `not_measured`. `checks.spf.score` is the same measurement in raw points (for example 11 of 15 there is 73 here); the two are not meant to agree numerically.

issues.description: What is wrong with this record, in sentences. Empty when nothing is.

selectors_found.description: Selectors that answered. Empty is the ordinary shape for a domain with no DKIM: the check probes a fixed list and cannot enumerate selectors.

policy.description: The `p=` value: `none`, `quarantine` or `reject`. `none` is published-but-not-enforcing, which scores worse than `quarantine` and better than nothing at all.

reputation.description: Blacklist standing. The counts are separate on purpose: a zone that did not answer is not a zone that cleared you.

score.description: **Null when fewer than half of `blacklists_total` gave a verdict and none listed the domain** (none at all, or, say, only the domain zones because no sending IP is known): there is no verdict to score, a 100 from the few that answered would read as a clean record, and a zero would read as "listed everywhere". A listing is scored whatever the coverage.

blacklists_checked.description: Zones that returned a usable answer.

blacklists_inconclusive.description: Zones that answered with something that could not be read as listed or not listed. **They are removed from the grade rather than scored against it**: `checkBlacklists` scales both the section score and its maximum by the consulted proportion, so an unreadable zone neither penalises the domain nor silently counts as clean; the reputation section simply carries less weight. That is why `score` here can be null when nothing answered at all.

blacklists_skipped.description: Zones not queried on this run.

blacklists_total.description: Zones in the list. `checked + inconclusive + skipped` should account for it.

blacklists_listed.description: Zones that reported the domain or its IP as listed.

listed_on.description: Which ones, and how much each matters. Empty when `blacklists_listed` is 0.

severity.description: How much a listing there costs, worst first.

server.description:
What a probe of the receiving server would have found. **Four of these five are always null**: `accepts_mail`, `response_time_ms`, `supports_tls` and `tls_version` are hard-coded null in the projection: no SMTP banner, TLS or acceptance probe runs on this route, with or without a `sending_ip`. Only `reverse_dns` is ever populated, from the PTR check, and only when a `sending_ip` was supplied.

Null here means "not measured", never "no". The fields exist because the shape is shared with a probe that may be added later; today they are placeholders and must not be reported as evidence about the server.

accepts_mail.description: Always null today: no acceptance probe runs. Not "the server refuses mail".

response_time_ms.description: Always null today: nothing is timed.

supports_tls.description: Always null today. Not "no TLS": nothing connected to find out.

tls_version.description: Always null today, for the same reason as `supports_tls`.

reverse_dns.description: The PTR record for the `sending_ip`, and the only field here that is ever populated. Null when no `sending_ip` was supplied, because `checkPtr` is handed the IP directly and returns `status: "skipped"` for null; it never resolves an address from the MX records.

spam_assessment.description: The same evidence again, expressed as how likely mail from this domain is to be filtered.

score.description: How likely mail from this domain is to be filtered, 0-100, where **higher is worse**. It is the INVERSE of the top-level `score`: `100 - score`, clamped. A domain scoring 90 for deliverability carries a spam score of 10. Do not compare it against the top-level number or apply the same thresholds to it.

spam_likelihood.description: A band, not a prediction about any one message. **Derived from the DELIVERABILITY score, not from `score` beside it**: `low` at 80 and above, `medium` from 60, `high` below. Because that sibling is the inverse, applying these numbers to it reads every domain backwards: a spam score of 10 is the best case, not the worst. Read `spam_likelihood` and leave the arithmetic alone. **null when `grade` is null**: the band is read off the same partial score, so it is withheld with the grade.

factors.description: What pushed the score each way, including the things that helped.

impact.description: Which way it pushed. `neutral` means it changed nothing: it was assessed with no effect, skipped (reverse DNS without a `sending_ip`, or too few blocklists answered to give a verdict), or not measured because its lookup failed. The `description` says which.

key_preview.description: `ev_****` and the key's last four characters, never the secret. An older key that has no stored preview shows `ev_••••`, with no characters from the key.

scopes.description: What this key may reach. **`null` means UNRESTRICTED**: every key created without a `scopes` array is, and that is the default. Always present, so `null` is a fact about the key rather than a field an older build omitted.

name.description: Optional: the handler assigns `name: user.name`, and `UserRecord.name` is itself optional, so JSON serialization omits the property entirely for an account that never stored one.

plan.description: The account's own plan. Never `sub_account`: a white-label sub-account's key gets the SubAccount shape instead, which is a different object.

created_at.description: The account creation time. Legacy rows that predate this field are returned as the empty string; the handler does not invent a timestamp.

email_delivery.description: Whether Kawaa is still willing to email this account. Always present, including the healthy case.

next_reset.description: When the allowance refills: the end of the billing period. Absent with no billing period, and absent when the plan is set to end at the close of this period (the account then moves to Free and the unspent allowance is removed). For a short time after a renewal, until its payment is recorded, `used_this_month` has not been reset and still includes the previous period's spend; `usage.period` then runs from the last reset up to now, and this is the moment the previous period ended.

allowance_basis.description: Whether the allowance renews. Only `billing_period` does, and not when the plan is set to end at the close of the period, which `next_reset` being absent says. `next_reset` alone cannot say why it is absent: it is also absent for every account with no billing period on file, Free and paid alike.

partial.description: Names sections that could NOT BE LOADED. Their values are placeholders, not facts. Do not render an empty state for a flagged section.

withheld.description: Names sections this API key's SCOPES DO NOT COVER. They come back empty; an empty api_keys here never means the account has no keys. `usage: true` means `usage.current_month` is ZERO-FILLED rather than measured, so a client that ignores this marker publishes a fabricated month of no activity.

AsyncVerifyOptions.description: Verification options for an ASYNCHRONOUS submission. Deliberately not `VerifyOptions`: that schema permits `timeout_ms`, which these routes refuse with 400 INVALID_OPTION because there is no synchronous wait to bound. Omit `options` to use the defaults; a present `null` is refused with the same code before work starts or credits are charged.

include_ai.description: Run the AI-assisted checks (default `true`). Turning it off does more than remove AI analysis. The built-in rules alone then answer the typo and catch-all checks, so `ai` and `suggestion` still appear when they find something. The worker also skips the SPF, DKIM and DMARC lookup, which runs only with this option on: `domain_info` then carries `auth_score`, `auth_grade`, `has_spf`, `spf_policy`, `has_dmarc`, `dmarc_policy` and `has_dkim` only when a recent check of the same domain already measured them, so expect them to be absent.

enrich.description: Include name, gender and country hints where available. Needs the Business plan or higher: on a lower plan the whole submission is refused with `403 PLAN_UPGRADE_REQUIRED` and nothing is charged.

JobResultsInline.description: `format=json` under the inline threshold. NOT the standard envelope: this route answers with the object itself, so there is no `success` or `data` wrapper to unwrap. Carries the completeness verdict: read `complete` before treating `results` as the job.

complete.description: Whether this export is the job's whole result set. `true` when the rows returned reach the job's own `processed_emails`; `false` when they fall short; `null` when the job row carries no count to compare against, which is "not verified" and never a stand-in for "complete". The export is read from an eventually-consistent index, so a job that has just finished can be exported before its last rows are visible: a short file that used to be reported as the job's results with nothing saying otherwise. Measured on the UNFILTERED read, so a `filter=` export inherits the verdict of the read it was narrowed from.

expected_rows.description: The job's `processed_emails` (how many addresses it finished), which is what the export was counted against. `null` when the job row carries none.

rows_missing.description: `expected_rows` minus the rows the read returned, or `0` when nothing is missing. `null` when completeness was not verified. Never negative: a read returning more than `processed_emails` is not short. Measured on the UNFILTERED read, like `complete`, so on a `filter=` export it counts the rows missing from the whole job, not from the filtered file: `result_count` can be far below `expected_rows` while `rows_missing` is `0`.

message.description: Present only when `complete` is not `true`. Says what is missing and what to do: normally request the download again in a few seconds, because the index catches up. A persistent shortfall means those rows aged out of the plan's data-retention window.

score.description: The quality score, named `score` in this shape.

catch_all.description: Whether a mailbox probe found an accept-everything domain. Omitted when no probe measured it (a disposable or spam-trap verdict, a DNS failure, a refused or unanswered mailbox, an inconclusive probe); absent is not `false`. In `format=csv` the cell is empty.

sub_status.description: The reason code behind `status`, the same value as `sub_status` on the verification result (see `SubStatus`; new values can be added). Omitted when the result has none, as on a disposable or spam-trap verdict whose DNS lookups answered; in `format=csv` the cell is empty. A disposable or spam-trap verdict whose DNS lookup failed carries `temporary_failure`: the verdict stands, but the domain checks beside it were not measured. The last column, so the columns before it keep their positions.

JobListItem.description: A row of the job listing: a `Job` plus the field that distinguishes an uploaded-file job.

filename.description: The uploaded file this job came from, or null for a job submitted as a list.

SubAccount.description: What `GET /v1/account` returns when the key belongs to a white-label sub-account. A sub-account has no plan, no allowance and no keys of its own: it spends a pool its parent allocated, so the credit fields are `allocated` and `credits_used` rather than `monthly_allowance` and `used_this_month`. Their absence is the shape of this account, not missing billing data.

plan.description: Always this. The parent's tier decides the limits; @see GET /v1/usage/limits, whose `plan_note` says where the inherited numbers come from.

limits_plan.description: The plan whose features and limits this sub-account has: its parent's, as it stood when the request was made. A sub-account never gets more than its parent's plan includes.

created_at.description: The sub-account creation time. Legacy rows that predate this field are returned as the empty string; the handler does not invent a timestamp.

parent_user_id.description: The account that provisioned this one and owns its credit pool.

balance.description: What is left of the allocation. Fractional: a cached verification costs 0.5.

allocated.description: What the parent has granted in total. `0` for a sub-account that has never been allocated any.

credits_used.description: Spend since provisioning: exactly `allocated - balance`, which is why it is published even for a key without the analytics scope: both operands are already here. This says nothing about `usage.current_month`, which is still withheld and still flagged.

usage.description: `current_month` and `period`, as on the parent shape.

requests_per_minute.description: The sub-account's own ceiling, inherited from the parent's tier.

partial.description: Names sections that could NOT BE LOADED. Their values are placeholders, not facts. No `api_keys` here: this response carries no such section.

withheld.description: Names sections this API key's SCOPES DO NOT COVER. `usage: true` means `usage.current_month` is ZERO-FILLED rather than measured. `api_keys: true` is always set here, because a sub-account has no key list to read.

BadRequest.description: The request is malformed, or names a field this endpoint does not accept. Retrying it unchanged will fail identically.

Unauthorized.description: No credential, or one that is not accepted. `code` distinguishes `API_KEY_SUSPENDED` (subscription ended; restartable) from `API_KEY_REVOKED`, `SESSION_EXPIRED` and `OAUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED` (a connected app's one-hour access token lapsed: refresh it and retry, or sign in again if no refresh token was issued or the refresh is refused).

Forbidden.description:
Refused, and **the code says which of three problems it is**, and they need different remedies:

- `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE`: the credential is valid but not scoped for this route. With an API key, issue one that carries the scope named in the message. With an OAuth access token, connect the app again asking for that scope as well as the ones it has, unless the message says a connected app can never be given it; then use an API key with every scope the message names, or have the account owner do it in the dashboard.
- `PLAN_UPGRADE_REQUIRED`: the account's plan does not include the feature. **No key of any scope reaches it**, so issuing another is wasted work; the remedy is a plan change. Returned by the verification routes for `options.enrich`, and by the finder, the monitors, the audit log, auto-clean and the white-label routes.
- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`: the plan includes the feature and the account is at its ceiling (webhook endpoints, team seats, integrations, auto-clean lists). Delete one or upgrade.
- `FORBIDDEN`: refused for a reason none of the above covers.

`ErrorCode` is an open set, so branch on the code with a default rather than exhaustively.

NotFound.description: No such resource on this account.

InsufficientCredits.description: The account cannot pay for this request. The message carries the numbers and where to top up. Nothing was charged.

IdempotencyConflict.description: The `Idempotency-Key` was used before for a different request on this route. No credit moved. Repeat the original request exactly, or use a new key.

PayloadTooLarge.description: The request body is over the limit.

RateLimited.description: Too many requests. When the server knows how long to wait, `Retry-After` says so and `error.retry_after_seconds` carries the same number; the `X-RateLimit-*` headers say where you stand.

ServiceUnavailable.description: Temporarily unable to serve; `error.retryable` says whether waiting cures it. On a credit-charging route a contended balance answers this too, not an empty wallet: that one charged nothing, so retry.

IdempotentJobExpired.description: `IDEMPOTENT_JOB_EXPIRED`, not retryable. The prior job for this `Idempotency-Key` has reached the end of the data-retention period of the plan it was submitted under (7 days on Free) while the key's receipt, kept at least 30 days, still stands. The job cannot be replayed or restarted from that receipt. This retry was not charged. Send a new key to run the request again.

tags.description:
Be told when work finishes instead of polling.

**Verifying a delivery.** Every signed delivery carries `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>`. `t` is when that request was sent and `v1` is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>` (the `t` string, a period, then the raw request body bytes), keyed with the webhook's secret: a registered endpoint's `secret`, or a job's `webhook_secret`. Recompute it over the raw body, compare it with a constant-time comparison, and refuse the request when `t` is more than 300 seconds from your clock in either direction (the recommended tolerance): a captured delivery then cannot be replayed later. A header may carry several `v1` entries (any match verifies); ignore entries with other names.

Each attempt is signed when it is sent, so an automatic retry, a manual retry (`POST /v1/webhooks/{id}/logs/{logId}/retry`) and a test delivery each carry a fresh `t`. Check the window against `t` only: the body's `timestamp` keeps the time of the original delivery, and `X-Kawaa-Timestamp` is informational and not signed.

`X-Kawaa-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body>` is the legacy signature, still sent unchanged for existing receivers. It signs no time, so a captured delivery verifies against it forever; verify `X-Kawaa-Signature-V2` instead. A per-job callback sent without a `webhook_secret` carries neither.
